flags: LifeStance reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $455.9 million and raised its full year 2026 outlook, with revenue guidance raised to $1.741 billion to $1.761 billion.

The company entered into an underwriting agreement for a secondary offering of 45,000,000 shares sold entirely by selling stockholders, and the company purchased 2,000,000 of those shares from the underwriters; the offering closed on November 12, 2026.

The company entered into an underwriting agreement for a secondary offering of 22,250,000 shares sold by selling stockholders and agreed to purchase 2,000,000 of those shares from the underwriter; the offering closed on September 11, 2026.
no_value_reason: no valuation route for this kind of company yet (real estate, pre-profit biotech)

business_model.claim: LifeStance earns revenue per visit, each time a patient receives care from one of its employed clinicians.
quotes: We generate revenue on a per-visit basis when a patient receives care from one of our clinicians.

business_model.claim: It sells outpatient mental health services, delivered virtually or in person: psychiatric evaluation and treatment, psychological and neuropsychological testing, and individual, family and group therapy.
quotes: Our clinicians offer patients a comprehensive, multidisciplinary suite of mental health services, spanning psychiatric evaluations and treatment, psychological and neuropsychological testing, and individual, family and group therapy.
Patients can receive care virtually through our online delivery platform or in-person at one of our conveniently located centers.

business_model.basis: stated in P1 and repeated in P3
business_model.claim: Commercial in-network insurers fund most revenue: in 2025, 90% of revenue came from commercial in-network payors, 5% from government payors, 4% from self-pay and 1% from non-patient services.
quotes: For the year ended December 31, 2025, 90% of our revenue was derived from patients with commercial in-network payors, 5% of our revenue was derived from patients with government payors, 4% of our revenue was derived from patients on a self-pay basis and 1% of our revenue was derived from non-patient services.

business_model.basis: stated in P1; risk framing in P2
business_model.claim: Payor contracts are typically fee-for-service, with negotiated reimbursement rates.
quotes: Our contracts with payors are typically structured as fee-for-service arrangements, with negotiated reimbursement rates for our clinical services.

business_model.claim: In states where clinicians work through supported practices, the company's revenue comes from management fees under long-term management services contracts.
quotes: With respect to our supported practices, our revenue is derived from management fees negotiated under our management services contracts.

business_model.claim: Revenue is concentrated in two payors: UnitedHealthcare and Elevance Health each exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue, at 14% and 15% respectively.
quotes: Two payors individually exceeded 10% of our total revenue for the year ended December 31, 2025: UnitedHealthcare and Elevance Health, Inc., comprising 14% and 15% of our total revenue, respectively.

business_model.claim: Visit capacity rests on the employed clinician base, which grew from 8,040 clinicians in 33 states at December 31, 2025 to 8,863 at September 30, 2026.
quotes: We employed 8,040 licensed mental health clinicians through our subsidiaries and supported practices in 33 states as of December 31, 2025.
As of September 30, 2026, we employed 8,863 psychiatrists, advanced practice nurses, psychologists and therapists through our subsidiaries and supported practices.

business_model.basis: stated in P6 (earnings release); F2 shows total revenue of 455,864 (table in thousands)
business_model.claim: Management attributes Q3 2026 revenue growth to three drivers: more visits from net clinician growth, better clinician productivity, and higher total revenue per visit. Revenue grew 25% to $455.9 million.
quotes: Revenue growth in the third quarter was driven primarily by higher visit volumes from net clinician growth, improved clinician productivity, and higher total revenue per visit.

business_model.claim: Visit volume rose 17% to 2.7 million in Q3 2026, with 7.8 million visits over the first nine months of 2026.
quotes: Third quarter visit volumes increased 17% to 2.7 million
Our clinicians treated patients through 2.7 million and 7.8 million visits in the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively.

business_model.claim: Clinician productivity depends on the time clinicians make available and on filling their schedules, and periods with fewer business days produce lower revenue.
quotes: We generate lower revenue and experience lower clinician productivity in periods that have fewer business days than other periods.

We measure productivity by the number of visits that are performed by a clinician, which is driven by the time clinicians make available to see patients and our ability to fill clinicians' schedules by attracting new patients, scheduling patients, and converting scheduled appointments to completed visits.

business_model.claim: New patients come through physician referral partners, internal clinician referrals, payor relationships and marketing.
quotes: We utilize multiple strategies to add new patients to our platform, including our primary care and specialist physician relationships, internal referrals from our clinicians, our payor relationships and our dedicated marketing efforts.

business_model.basis: stated in P4; figures from F2. That clinician pay sits in center costs is inferred from P3's Center Margin definition, under which center costs are the direct costs of delivering care
business_model.claim: The largest cost is clinician compensation, which is mainly driven by each clinician's visit count. It sits within center costs, which were 294,462 in Q3 2026 versus 247,227 in Q3 2025 (table in thousands).
quotes: Clinician productivity impacts our ability to generate revenue and also impacts clinician compensation, as clinician compensation is primarily driven by the number of visits provided by each clinician.
Center costs, excluding depreciation and amortization shown separately below

business_model.basis: definition stated in P3 footnote; figures from F2
business_model.claim: General and administrative expense covers leadership, finance, HR, marketing, billing, credentialing, technology infrastructure and all stock-based compensation. It was 113,389 in Q3 2026 versus 95,615 in Q3 2025 (table in thousands).
quotes: Represents salaries, wages and employee benefits for our executive leadership, finance, human resources, marketing, billing and credentialing support and technology infrastructure and stock-based compensation for all employees.

business_model.basis: definition stated in P3; figures stated in P6
business_model.claim: Management uses Center Margin (operating income excluding D&A and G&A) to track the economics of delivering care. Q3 2026 Center Margin was 161,402 (table in thousands), or 35.4% of revenue versus 32.0%.
quotes: We define Center Margin as income (loss) from operations excluding depreciation and amortization and general and administrative expenses.

business_model.claim: Management attributes Q3 2026 margin expansion to higher revenue per visit, lower center costs as a share of revenue, and revenue growing faster than G&A.
quotes: Adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of revenue increased in the third quarter as a result of higher total revenue per visit, lower center costs as a percentage of revenue, and improved operating leverage from revenue growing faster than general and administrative expenses.

business_model.claim: Labor costs have risen because of the higher wages and benefits needed to attract and retain clinicians.
quotes: As we implement actions to reduce attrition and increase hiring of clinicians, we have experienced increases in our labor costs, primarily due to higher wages and greater benefits required to retain and attract qualified healthcare personnel, and such increases may adversely affect our profitability.

business_model.claim: Costs may not fall in line with revenue: lower volume or reimbursement can cut revenue while expenses, including clinician compensation, stay higher.
quotes: In some cases, our revenue decreases if our volume or reimbursement decreases, but our expenses, including clinician compensation, may not decrease proportionately.

business_model.basis: stated in P3 and P4; counter from P2
business_model.claim: The company says it has historically obtained the same reimbursement rate for virtual and in-person visits, either by contract or under payor policy.
quotes: The strength of our payor relationships and our value proposition has historically allowed us to secure rate parity between in-person and virtual visits, either by contract or payor policy.

quotes: Planning Assumptions Assumes 20 to 30 new center openings

quotes: Two payors individually exceeded 10% of our total revenue for the year ended December 31, 2025: UnitedHealthcare and Elevance Health, Inc., comprising 14% and 15% of our total revenue, respectively.

risks.basis: Stated in the 10-K risk factors and MD&A (P2, P3), set against the Q3 release (P6).
risks.claim: Revenue depends on commercial reimbursement: 90% of 2025 revenue came from commercial in-network payors, so lower rates or reduced coverage would hurt results.
quotes: If any commercial third-party payors reduce their reimbursement rates or elect not to cover some or all of our services, our business, results of operations and financial condition may be harmed.

A majority of our revenue is derived from patients with commercial in-network insurance coverage – for the year ended December 31, 2025, our payor mix by revenue was 90% commercial in-network payors, 5% government payors, 4% self-pay and 1% non-patient services revenue.

risks.basis: Stated in the 10-K risk factors and MD&A (P2, P3).
risks.claim: Telehealth reimbursement parity is not guaranteed by law, because less than half of states require it, so virtual visits could be paid less than in-person visits.
quotes: We operate in states that have not adopted laws related to parity between reimbursement rates for virtual services and in-person care, as presently less than half of states require reimbursement of payment parity for telehealth.
The strength of our payor relationships and our value proposition has historically allowed us to secure rate parity between in-person and virtual visits, either by contract or payor policy.
